title_original: The Met’s Orientalism Exhibition Puts Edward Said on Display—and His Critique Aside
excerpt_original: Far from confronting the ideological premises of Orientalist representation, the exhibition seems to render them newly respectable.

blocks.text: I have been teaching a graduate seminar on Orientalism and representation at MIT for the last 34 years. Centered around Edward Said’s 1978 book Orientalism , the course examines the ways fraught relationships between the “West” and the “Orient” have been represented across different media since at least the Renaissance. Every two years, as I prepare to teach the seminar anew, I ask myself whether it might be time to shelve the subject, which has become so mainstream and seemingly overanalyzed. And every two years, something happens on the world stage that convinces me it’s still necessary.

This year, in addition to the rising racism against Muslims and Arabs in European and American political discourse; the vilification of Palestinians, Yemenis, and Iranians in Western media as their homelands are being destroyed; the suppression of Muslim rights in Modi’s India; and the continuing erasure of Muslim identities in Myanmar and China, an exhibition enigmatically titled “Orientalism: Between Fact and Fantasy” has reaffirmed the urgency of Said’s critique of Orientalism as a “Western style for dominating, restructuring, and having authority over the Orient.” I will be teaching the seminar again next fall.

The exhibition, on view at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York until February 28, is the latest in a succession of exhibitions devoted to Orientalist art mounted around the world over the past three decades. As such, it introduces little material that has not already appeared in similar contexts, highlighting celebrated 19th-century Orientalist painters, principally Jean-Léon Gérôme (1824–1904) and Osman Hamdi Bey (1842–1910), among orientalizing 19th-century vases, plates, lamps, and ewers; old photos of “Orientals” and the Orient; and a number of representations of bashi-bozouks , the general term Europeans used to designate the unruly and reckless irregulars in Oriental armies.

blocks.caption: Jean-Léon Gérôme: The Snake Charmer , ca. 1879. Courtesy Clark Art Institute, Williamstown, Mass.

blocks.text: Yet, to my mind, its most ingenious maneuver is the way it manages to circumvent nearly half a century of sustained criticism of Orientalism without openly challenging that criticism. Indeed, it even enshrines the first hardcover edition of Said’s Orientalism , with its famous cover reproducing Gérôme’s The Snake Charmer (1879), as a fetish object in a glass case alongside three Turkish helmets without incorporating its arguments into its texts. The rest of that gallery is largely devoted to dissecting Gérôme’s controversial painting, explaining where the artist might have found his visual sources.

A TELLING OMMISSION transpires at the entrance connecting the museum’s Islamic galleries to the Orientalist exhibition, where the arrangement, to my eyes, suggests considerably more than the wall text explicitly states. Two glass cases flank the opening. On the left is a copy of Pascal Coste’s Architecture arabe: ou, Monuments du Kaire, mesurés et dessinés, de 1818 à 1826 (1837–39); on the right, a volume of the monumental Description de l’Égypte , the multivolume encyclopedic survey (published between 1809 and 1829) that was produced by the army of scholars and scientists who accompanied Napoleon’s ill-fated invasion of Egypt (1798–1801). Together, the volumes invoke one of the exhibition’s principal themes: In the 19th century, Orientalism produced knowledge. Yet the critique—“knowledge is power”—on which Said, following Michel Foucault, insisted, goes unmentioned.

Meanwhile, the two paintings hanging above the cases make that power relationship unmistakable to the attentive viewer. Painted by Gérôme more than 60 years after the failure of the invasion and more than 40 years after Napoleon’s death, they belong to a series of hagiographic representations of Bonaparte in Egypt. One depicts Napoleon on horseback surveying Cairo, the city he conquered, from the ramparts of its Citadel. The other shows him defiantly confronting the Sphinx. Taken together, the paintings proclaim French dominion over Egypt’s present and past, precisely the ambition underlying Napoleon’s first colonial venture into the Orient.

That they were painted around the time of the contentious renegotiations between Isma ʿ il Pasha, Egypt’s ruler (1863–79), and the French-dominated Suez Canal Company, headed by Ferdinand de Lesseps (1805–94), may be more than coincidental. Those negotiations culminated in an inequitable compensation settlement imposed on Egypt through the arbitration of Napoleon III, who regarded the canal as a prestige project for the Second French Empire. Gérôme’s resurrection of Napoleon I’s Egyptian campaign, at a moment when France was consolidating its economic and political influence over Egypt, had a charge that would hardly have escaped his contemporaneous French audience. None of this historical context, however, is mentioned in the exhibition.

blocks.caption: View of the exhibition “Orientalism: Between Fact and Fantasy,” 2026–27, at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Photo Anna-Marie Kellen/Courtesy the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

blocks.text: If France’s imperial ambitions in Egypt were primarily financial and economic exploitation, its colonization of Algeria was considerably more direct and brutal. Following the invasion of 1830, French armies spent decades attempting to suppress Algerian resistance, most prominently that led by Emir ʿ Abd al-Qādir al-Jazā ʾ irī, represented here in a melancholy photographic portrait taken in 1860 by the Parisian firm Mayer & Pierson. The caption cryptically states that he “was the spiritual and military leader of Algeria following the French invasion of the country in 1830” and that “hoping to end his people’s suffering, he surrendered in 1847, living as a prisoner in France.”

What precisely was the emir doing as a leader? Who was responsible for his people’s suffering? What circumstances compelled him to surrender, and why was he subsequently imprisoned? The caption hints at these questions without answering them, leaving me wondering how a visitor unfamiliar with the history of French colonialism could possibly make sense of such evasive formulations, which transform a protracted struggle against conquest into an almost inexplicable sequence of personal decisions and misfortunes.

In reality, in 1843, French forces launched a surprise attack on his smala , the mobile encampment that housed his family and followers. The raid caused numerous casualties, including noncombatants; resulted in the capture of members of the emir’s household; and led to the seizure of his possessions and library while he was absent.

blocks.caption: Jean-Léon Gérôme: Dance of the Almeh , 1863. Courtesy Dayton Art Institute

blocks.text: THE PAINTER ACCORDED the greatest prominence and most profuse praise in the exhibition is Osman Hamdi Bey, a member of the Ottoman ruling elite who was born in Constantinople, educated in France, and served as director of the Imperial Museum. He also led several archaeological expeditions in the Arab provinces of the empire, and, most significantly for this exhibition, emerged as the foremost Ottoman practitioner of Orientalist painting. Over the past three decades, largely Turkish scholars have elevated him into the paradoxical figure of an anti-Orientalist Orientalist, an artist supposedly capable of overturning the conventions of a genre whose techniques and subjects he enthusiastically adopted.

But the contrast between his and Gérôme’s paintings and themes hardly amounts to a critique of Orientalism. Hamdi’s major paintings are often cerebral, enigmatic, and resistant to straightforward interpretation. Some, such as The Tortoise Trainer (1906) and The Mihrab (Genesis) (1901), neither included in the exhibition, border on the insulting in their treatment of Islamic sensibilities. Others, including his various depictions of reading emirs and young women, examples of which are on view, are celebrated for reversing a familiar Orientalist trope: The supposedly indolent and ignorant Orientals are shown instead as learned individuals absorbed in books. Between these opposites stand his depictions of urban life in Istanbul and Bursa, praised by the curators as “vibrant,” “dynamic,” and—most perplexingly—“modern.”

blocks.caption: Osman Hamdi Bey: At the Mosque Door , 1879. Courtesy Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York

blocks.text: This last characterization stopped me in my tracks, particularly as I examined Hamdi’s celebrated At the Mosque Door (1891). The painting depicts groups before the portal to the Muradiye Mosque in Bursa (1425–26). Hamdi-like figures, dressed in various forms of traditional attire, are scattered across the scene: a seated mendicant, a sheikh, a man apparently preparing for ablution, and perhaps a vendor of books and calligraphic panels. Several figures resemble Hamdi himself; this is a recurring feature in his paintings. But the most incongruous, indeed awkward, elements of the composition are two groups of women: Two stand on a stone porch to the left of the entrance, and four ascend the steps toward the mosque. Elegantly dressed in fashionable Ottoman entaris , several carrying delicate parasols, they appear to have been transposed from a leisurely promenade in a park to the threshold of a mosque. Nothing in their demeanor or the composition convincingly suggests that they are entering the building, participating in its activities, or even particularly interested in their architectural surroundings. They seem less integrated into the setting than inserted into it.

The exhibition label declares that Hamdi’s portrayals of Islam and the mosque as public space “emphasize daily life and articulate a sense of authenticity and modernity.” Is it the women theatrically approaching the mosque, perhaps, who are the source of the authenticity and modernity found in the painting? Their presence would have been unusual given the social norms of the time.

I could not help recalling the photographs that circulated not long ago on social media of Afghan and Iranian women strolling through their cities in short skirts during the 1970s, presented as incontrovertible evidence that these societies had once been “modern,” before the imposition of stricter dress codes by the mullahs and the Taliban. In these images, modernity is reduced to a woman’s appearance and freedom of dress, abstracted from the political, economic, and social conditions in which she lived. Might Hamdi Bey’s clumsily staged women, and the exhibition’s enthusiastic reading of them, be reproducing a similarly reductive understanding of modernity? More fundamentally, why should the insertion of fashionable women into an otherwise straightforward Orientalist painting make it modern?

I left the exhibition with the disquieting impression that Orientalism, as Said defined and critiqued it, is being expertly resurrected, aesthetically rehabilitated, and intellectually retrofitted for our troubling times of suspicion, intolerance, and rejection of the different other. Far from confronting the ideological premises of Orientalist representation, the exhibition seems to render them newly respectable under the ostensibly neutral rubrics of artistic achievement, historical curiosity, and knowledge production. That this rehabilitation should occur at a moment when the peoples once objectified by Orientalism are again subjected to dehumanization, dispossession, and violence makes the exhibition’s evasions all the more troubling—and the critique of Orientalism all the more necessary.
